catalog_quote: In Maskelynes stress is difficult to detect and differences are not particularly pronounced. ... All things being equal, Maskelynes still gives the appearance of having an underlying system of penultimate stress with alternate preceding syllables also being stressed. However, things are very rarely equal. ... for forms ending with CVCV(C)# with identical vowels in the last two syllables, impressionistically 44/45 CVCV# forms and 91/98 CVCVC# forms are stressed on the penultimate syllable. But this is not the case when vowels are different. In the lexicon, for stems of two or more syllables, those syllables with non-high vowels as nucleus are stressed in 97% of cases (n=561) regardless of syllable shape or whether the syllable is penultimate or ultimate. In terms of weight this means that syllables containing non-high vowels are ranked as heavier than those containing high vowels. ... As a result of these figures it is possible to give a finer ranking of syllable weight, as follows: non-high (a > e, o) > high (i, u > ə) ... Stress seems to be assigned from the right margin of the word following the non-high vowel > high vowel weighting, and then the finer gradations of weighting. Apparently the finer gradations of weight can be overruled by sentence initial and sentence final intonation. ... In summary, stress is usually assigned according to the weight of the syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weak (cued mainly by intensity) and is assigned by syllable weight, where weight is determined by vowel quality, not by codas: non-high vowels (a > e, o) outrank high vowels (i, u > ə). Scanning from the right edge of the word, stress goes to the heavier of the final syllables; when the last two vowels are identical the default is penultimate (44/45 CVCV#, 91/98 CVCVC#), so a final /a/ after a penultimate high or mid vowel takes final stress (e.g. /pe.ˈlan/ 'tomorrow', /si.ˈpa/ 'thanks') while /ˈsa.rex/ 'deep', /ˈa.kis/ 'always' are penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Other stressed syllables (alternate preceding syllables in the default pattern, or other heavy/non-high-vowel syllables) carry secondary stress; the rightmost stressed syllable is marked primary, though acoustically primary does not consistently have more 'energy' than secondary (p. 34); e.g. /ˌa.so.ˈan/ 'his/her spouse', /ˌmʷor.ˈmʷo.ri/ 'round', /ˌna.ˌsor.xu.su.ri.ˈan/ 'paying attention'.
new_statements.exceptions: When the final two syllables have similar weight a single speaker may stress either (/ˈxa.ᵐbat/ ~ /xa.ˈᵐbat/ 'very', /ˈa.le/ ~ /a.ˈle/ 'OK'); sentence-initial and sentence-final intonation can override the finer weight gradations (/e.ˈnan/ medially vs /ˈe.nan/ initially 'that'); reduplicated CVC syllables both tend to be stressed, sometimes with an epenthetic schwa; in derived words stress may follow the root's verbal pattern or the whole word (pragmatic choice); transitiviser hən-i recorded with stress on either syllable; author notes a change may be underway and that a Nahavaq-style 'no fixed word stress' analysis (Dimock 2009) is a conceivable alternative. 258/268 words in two texts (96%) fit the weight ranking.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; evidence from 174 nouns recorded in a frame clause plus all words of two recorded natural texts; interaction with sentence-level intonation noted explicitly. Schwa occurs almost only in unstressed syllables (p. 14).
new_statements.identity_note: Healey 2013 describes the language of Uluveu (Uliveo) Island in the Maskelyne group, fieldwork based mainly in Pelog (Pellonk) village with checking by speakers of all three villages; this is Glottolog mask1242 / ISO klv itself (Ray's 1926 'Kuliviu' is the same language). No dialect split is at issue.
